steps.text: Tell a parent, a teacher or another adult you trust.
If something seems unsafe, tell your supervisor or shift leader. If you get hurt, tell your employer right away.

src.t: OSHA, Safe Work for Young Workers

src2.t: California, I was injured at work

steps.text: Keep records of what happens. The EEOC says to include the names, phone numbers and addresses of anyone who saw it.
Call one of the offices below with your adult. Some deadlines are as short as 30 days, so do not wait.

start.note: Employers cannot punish you for speaking up (see section 5). These offices answer questions about work. If someone is hurt right now, get help from an adult near you first.

sections.title: 1. Your right to a safe workplace and training
sections.plain: OSHA says young workers have the right to a safe place to work and to safety training they can understand. Employers must pay for most required safety gear. Ask questions if something seems unsafe. New York's youth page says a worker can say no to a task that risks serious injury or death. The California pages we read talk about safety, heat and training, but do not say in plain words that a teen may refuse unsafe work. The Georgia and Illinois youth pages we read do not list a right to safe work or training for teens, so this page does not claim one for those states.

points.text: OSHA lists a safe workplace as a right of young workers.
points.quote: Work in a safe place.
points.source: US OSHA, Safe Work for Young Workers

points.text: OSHA says workers should get safety training in a language they understand.
points.quote: Receive safety and health training in a language that you understand.
points.source: US OSHA, Safe Work for Young Workers

points.text: OSHA says you can ask questions when something seems unsafe.
points.quote: Ask questions if you don't understand instructions or if something seems unsafe.
points.source: US OSHA, Safe Work for Young Workers

points.text: OSHA says you should be trained on required safety gear.
points.quote: Use and be trained on required safety gear, such as hard hats, goggles and ear plugs.
points.source: US OSHA, Safe Work for Young Workers

points.text: OSHA says the employer must tell you what to do if you get hurt.
points.quote: Tell you what to do if you get hurt on the job.
points.source: US OSHA, Safe Work for Young Workers

points.text: OSHA says employers pay for most safety gear.
points.quote: Employers must also pay for most types of required safety gear.
points.source: US OSHA, Parents and Educators

points.text: OSHA says you can file a confidential complaint about a serious hazard.
points.quote: File a confidential complaint with OSHA if you believe there is a serious hazard or that your employer is not following OSHA standards.
points.source: US OSHA, Safe Work for Young Workers

points.text: OSHA tells young workers to report unsafe conditions to a supervisor.
points.quote: Report unsafe conditions to a shift/team leader or supervisor.
points.source: US OSHA, Safe Work for Young Workers

points.text: For parents: OSHA says to help your teen report hazards, and to OSHA if needed.
points.quote: Help your young worker report hazards to managers or, if necessary, to OSHA if a work environment seems unsafe.
points.source: US OSHA, Parents and Educators

points.text: New York lists a safe workplace in its Youth Workers Bill of Rights.
points.quote: You have the right to a safe workplace
points.source: New York State Department of Labor, Youth Worker Information Hub

points.text: New York says a young worker may say no to a task that risks serious injury or death.
points.quote: If your employer asks you to do something that poses a risk of serious injury or death you have the right to say no.
points.source: New York State Department of Labor, Youth Worker Information Hub

points.text: California's July 2026 release says young workers may be especially at risk from heat, and says heat rules include training.
points.quote: Young workers may be especially vulnerable
points.source: California Department of Industrial Relations, News Release 2026-59

points.text: California says safety complaints can be filed confidentially (page lists Cal/OSHA 833-579-0927).
points.quote: Complaints about workplace safety and health hazards can be filed confidentially with
points.source: California Department of Industrial Relations, News Release 2026-59

points.text: Georgia's child labor FAQ says the child labor rules exist to keep minors safe. It does not list a teen right to safety training.
points.quote: ensure the safety of minors in the work place.
points.source: Georgia Department of Labor, Individuals FAQs, Child Labor

sections.title: 2. Jobs under 18 may not do
sections.plain: Federal law sets 18 as the minimum age for jobs the Secretary of Labor calls hazardous. The US Department of Labor page lists these in plain words: meat slicers and similar machines, power woodworking machines, balers and trash compactors, forklifts and similar lifting equipment, bakery machines, metal-forming machines, power saws, roofing, driving as a job, explosives, demolition, mining, radioactive materials, brick and tile making, trenching deeper than four feet, and logging or sawmills. Some of these have narrow exceptions, so the page uses words like generally and most. Ages 14 and 15 have extra limits. Georgia, Illinois and New York have their own lists too.

points.text: The 18-year minimum age for hazardous nonfarm jobs.
points.quote: The FLSA establishes an 18-year minimum age for those nonagricultural occupations
points.source: US DOL Wage and Hour Division, Fact Sheet 43 (revised December 2016)

points.text: Ages 14 and 15 also cannot do the hazardous jobs.
points.quote: Child Labor Regulation No. 3 also bans 14- and 15-year-olds from performing any work proscribed by the HOs.
points.source: US DOL Wage and Hour Division, Fact Sheet 43

points.text: The federal fact sheet lists 17 Hazardous Occupations Orders. One of them covers roofing.
points.quote: Roofing operations and work performed on or about a roof
points.source: US DOL Wage and Hour Division, Fact Sheet 43

points.text: No meat slicers, saws or choppers.
points.quote: Kids under 18 cannot operate power-driven meat processing machines, such as meat slicers, saws and meat choppers
points.source: US DOL Wage and Hour Division, What jobs are off limits

points.text: No power woodworking machines.
points.quote: Kids under 18 cannot operate power-driven woodworking machines, including chain saws, nailing machines and sanders.
points.source: US DOL Wage and Hour Division, What jobs are off limits

points.text: No balers or trash compactors.
points.quote: Kids under 18 cannot operate balers, compactors (including trash compactors)
points.source: US DOL Wage and Hour Division, What jobs are off limits

points.text: No forklifts and similar lifting equipment (page says most).
points.quote: Kids under 18 cannot operate, ride, or help use most power-driven hoisting apparatus
points.source: US DOL Wage and Hour Division, What jobs are off limits

points.text: Bakery machines are off limits.
points.quote: Kids under 18 generally cannot operate, clean or repair power-driven bakery machines
points.source: US DOL Wage and Hour Division, What jobs are off limits

points.text: Metal forming, punching and shearing machines are off limits.
points.quote: Kids under 18 cannot operate power-driven metal-working machines, including forming, punching and shearing machines.
points.source: US DOL Wage and Hour Division, What jobs are off limits

points.text: Power saws are off limits.
points.quote: Kids under 18 cannot operate or help on power-driven circular saws, band saws, guillotine shears, chain saws
points.source: US DOL Wage and Hour Division, What jobs are off limits

points.text: Roofing is off limits, even work on the ground.
points.quote: Kids under 18 cannot do most jobs in roofing operations, including work performed on the ground
points.source: US DOL Wage and Hour Division, What jobs are off limits

points.text: Driving as a job is generally off limits.
points.quote: Kids under 18 generally cannot drive motor vehicles or work outside the vehicle as a driver's helper
points.source: US DOL Wage and Hour Division, What jobs are off limits

points.text: Places that make or store explosives are generally off limits.
points.quote: Kids under 18 generally cannot work where explosives are manufactured or stored.
points.source: US DOL Wage and Hour Division, What jobs are off limits

points.text: Demolition is off limits.
points.quote: Kids under 18 cannot do jobs in wrecking, demolition and ship-breaking operations.
points.source: US DOL Wage and Hour Division, What jobs are off limits

points.text: Radioactive materials are off limits.
points.quote: Kids under 18 cannot do jobs where they are exposed to radioactive substances and ionizing radiation.
points.source: US DOL Wage and Hour Division, What jobs are off limits

points.text: Trenches deeper than four feet are off limits.
points.quote: working in a trench more than four feet deep
points.source: US DOL Wage and Hour Division, What jobs are off limits

points.text: Georgia: 14 and 15 year olds can only do jobs on the state's allowed list.
points.quote: Any job not specifically permitted for 14 and 15 year-olds, as listed below, is prohibited.
points.source: Georgia Department of Labor, Child Labor Hazardous Occupations

points.text: Georgia says its hazardous list is based on federal law.
points.quote: The state definition of child labor hazardous occupations is based on federal law.
points.source: Georgia Department of Labor, Child Labor Hazardous Occupations

points.text: New York says workers under 18 cannot be given jobs the law calls too dangerous.
points.quote: Workers under 18 years old cannot be hired or asked to do jobs the law says are too dangerous for young people.
points.source: New York State Department of Labor, Youth Worker Information Hub

points.text: Illinois has its own list of hazardous jobs and workplaces for minors (the Illinois page frames its Child Labor Law as protecting workers under 16).
points.quote: There are 27 specific occupations, and 7 specific workplaces, which are considered "hazardous" or inappropriate for employment of minors.
points.source: Illinois Department of Labor, Child Labor Law FAQ

points.text: Illinois compliance page example from its list.
points.quote: in construction work, including demolition and repair;
points.source: Illinois Department of Labor, Child Labor Law Compliance

sections.title: 3. Harassment and discrimination: what it is and how to report it
sections.plain: The EEOC runs a youth section for teen workers. Its page says the laws protect you from being harassed by anyone in your workplace. Harassment is unwelcome behavior based on things like race, color, religion or sex. To break the law, it has to be severe (very serious) or happen often. The EEOC youth pages say to tell the person to stop if you feel comfortable, tell a manager, talk to a parent or another adult, keep records, and file with the EEOC. The EEOC deadline is generally 180 calendar days, and longer in some places. The EEOC pages we read do not state a minimum age. California's civil rights agency gives a three year deadline. New York's youth page says harassment based on race or ethnicity is against the law. The Georgia youth pages we read do not cover harassment. The Illinois Department of Labor page lists the number for the Illinois Department of Human Rights.

points.text: What harassment is.
points.quote: Harassment is unwelcome conduct that is based on race, color, religion, sex
points.source: US EEOC, Harassment

points.text: Protection covers anyone who harasses you at work, on the EEOC's youth page.
points.quote: The laws enforced by EEOC protect you from being harassed by anyone in your workplace.
points.source: US EEOC, Youth Harassment FAQs

points.text: When it becomes illegal.
points.quote: the conduct must either be severe (meaning very serious) or pervasive (meaning that it occurred frequently)
points.source: US EEOC, Youth Harassment FAQs

points.text: Step: tell the person to stop if you feel okay doing that.
points.quote: If you feel comfortable, tell the person harassing you to stop.
points.source: US EEOC, Tips for Youth @ Work

points.text: Step: tell a manager.
points.quote: Report the behavior to your manager or another manager in your company.
points.source: US EEOC, Tips for Youth @ Work

points.text: Step: talk to a trusted adult.
points.quote: Talk to your parents, teachers, or another adult.
points.source: US EEOC, Tips for Youth @ Work

points.text: Step: keep records.
points.quote: Keep records including witness names, telephone numbers and addresses.
points.source: US EEOC, Tips for Youth @ Work

points.text: Step: file with the EEOC.
points.quote: File a complaint with the EEOC.
points.source: US EEOC, Tips for Youth @ Work

points.text: EEOC filing deadline.
points.quote: In general, you need to file a charge within 180 calendar days from the day the discrimination took place.
points.source: US EEOC, Time Limits For Filing A Charge

points.text: The deadline can be longer.
points.quote: The 180 calendar day filing deadline is extended to 300 calendar days
points.source: US EEOC, Time Limits For Filing A Charge

points.text: California: harassment is banned even at very small workplaces.
points.quote: Harassment is prohibited in all workplaces, even those with fewer than five employees.
points.source: California Civil Rights Department, Employment

points.text: California: how to start a complaint.
points.quote: Start by filing an “Intake Form.”
points.source: California Civil Rights Department, Employment

points.text: California: complaint deadline.
points.quote: must be filed within three years from the date an alleged discriminatory act occurred
points.source: California Civil Rights Department, Employment

points.text: New York lists a discrimination free workplace as a right of youth workers.
points.quote: You have the right to a discrimination-free workplace
points.source: New York State Department of Labor, Youth Worker Information Hub

points.text: New York says harassment because of race or ethnicity is against the law.
points.quote: It is against the law to be treated unfairly or harassed at your job because of your race or ethnicity
points.source: New York State Department of Labor, Youth Worker Information Hub

points.text: New York: how to file a complaint with its labor department.
points.quote: You can file a complaint with the Department of Labor by filling out this form:
points.source: New York State Department of Labor, Youth Worker Information Hub

sections.title: 4. If you get hurt: report it right away
sections.plain: Tell your boss about any injury as soon as you can. Many states give a deadline after which you can lose benefits: 30 days in California, Georgia and New York, and 45 days in Illinois. Workers' compensation is the system that pays for care after a job injury. State by state: California's glossary says employee includes minors. New York's booklet for minors says it covers minors and pays double if a minor is hurt while working illegally. Georgia's Supervisor's Manual (July 2019) says employee includes minors. Illinois' handbook does not mention minors, but the Illinois Act says compensation goes up 50 percent for a worker under 16 who is illegally employed. The Georgia documents are dated July 2019 and the Illinois handbook is dated January 2013, so ask the state office if the rule has changed.

points.text: California: tell your supervisor fast.
points.quote: Make sure your supervisor is notified of your injury as soon as possible.
points.source: California DIR, Division of Workers' Compensation, I was injured at work

points.text: California: 30 day warning.
points.quote: If you don’t report your injury within 30 days, you could lose your right to receive workers’ compensation benefits.
points.source: California DIR, Division of Workers' Compensation, I was injured at work

points.text: California: employer pays for medical care. (The page does not mention minors.)
points.quote: Medical care must be paid for by your employer if you get hurt on the job
points.source: California DIR, Division of Workers' Compensation, I was injured at work

points.text: California: minors count as employees in the DWC glossary.
points.quote: The term employee includes undocumented workers and minors.
points.source: California DIR, Division of Workers' Compensation, Glossary

points.text: Georgia: report right away and no later than 30 days (Employee Handbook, July 2019).
points.quote: You must report any accident immediately, but not later than 30 days after the accident, to your employer
points.source: Georgia State Board of Workers' Compensation, Employee Handbook

points.text: Georgia FAQ: waiting too long can cost benefits.
points.quote: If you wait longer than 30 days, you may lose your benefits.
points.source: Georgia State Board of Workers' Compensation, Law FAQs

points.text: Georgia: employers with three or more workers need coverage. The FAQ page does not mention minors.
points.quote: any business with three or more workers, including regular part-time workers
points.source: Georgia State Board of Workers' Compensation, Law FAQs

points.text: Georgia: the Supervisor's Manual (July 2019) says employee includes minors.
points.quote: “Employee” generally means every person, including minors, in the service of another
points.source: Georgia State Board of Workers' Compensation, Supervisor's Manual (July 2019)

points.text: New York: workers' compensation covers an injured minor.
points.quote: Workers’ Compensation is payable when a minor is injured in any way in the course of his or her employment.
points.source: New York State Department of Labor, Laws Governing the Employment of Minors (P882, 01/26)

points.text: New York: report in writing right away.
points.quote: An injured youngster should report the accident immediately and in writing to his or her employer or foreman.
points.source: New York State Department of Labor, Laws Governing the Employment of Minors (P882, 01/26)

points.text: New York: medical care is paid even with no lost time.
points.quote: Medical benefits are payable regardless of whether the employee has lost time from the job
points.source: New York State Department of Labor, Laws Governing the Employment of Minors (P882, 01/26)

points.text: New York: double pay if the minor was working in violation of the law.
points.quote: his or her compensation is double the regular award
points.source: New York State Department of Labor, Laws Governing the Employment of Minors (P882, 01/26)

points.text: New York: the employer pays the cost, not the worker.
points.quote: The cost of providing workers’ compensation insurance must be met entirely by the employer.
points.source: New York State Department of Labor, Laws Governing the Employment of Minors (P882, 01/26)

points.text: New York youth page: a 30 day warning about telling your employer you were hurt.
points.quote: If you do not let your employer know you were injured at work within 30 days
points.source: New York State Department of Labor, Youth Worker Information Hub

points.text: Illinois: 45 day outer limit to tell the employer. The handbook does not mention minors.
points.quote: Generally, the employee must notify the employer as soon as practicable, but no later than 45 days after the accident.
points.source: Illinois Workers' Compensation Commission, Handbook on Workers' Compensation

points.text: Illinois Act: compensation rises 50 percent for a worker under 16 who is illegally employed.
points.quote: the injured employee is under 16 years of age at the time of the accident and is illegally employed
points.source: Illinois Workers' Compensation Act, Section 7(h)

sections.title: 5. Punishment for speaking up (retaliation)
sections.plain: Employers cannot punish you for using your safety or workplace rights. OSHA, the Department of Labor, the EEOC, California, New York and Illinois all say so on pages we read. If you think you were punished for speaking up, the OSHA page says deadlines vary and can be as short as 30 days, so act fast. The Georgia youth and workers' compensation pages we read do not address retaliation, so this page makes no Georgia claim about it.

points.text: OSHA: safety rights come without punishment.
points.quote: Exercise your workplace safety rights without retaliation or discrimination.
points.source: US OSHA, Safe Work for Young Workers

points.text: OSHA: you can file a whistleblower complaint.
points.quote: You have the right to file a whistleblower complaint with OSHA if you believe your employer retaliated against you
points.source: US OSHA, File a Complaint

points.text: OSHA: the deadline can be short.
points.quote: Filing deadline is 30-180 days (deadlines vary with each statute)
points.source: US OSHA, File a Complaint

points.text: US Department of Labor: no punishment for using your rights.
points.quote: An employer cannot retaliate against a worker for exercising their rights
points.source: US DOL Wage and Hour Division, YouthRules

points.text: US Department of Labor: what an adverse action is.
points.quote: would dissuade a reasonable employee from raising a concern
points.source: US DOL Wage and Hour Division, Retaliation

points.text: EEOC: you cannot be punished for reporting discrimination.
points.quote: you cannot legally be punished or fired for reporting job discrimination.
points.source: US EEOC, Tips for Youth @ Work

points.text: California: no punishment for a job injury.
points.quote: It’s illegal for your employer to punish or fire you for having a job injury
points.source: California DIR, Division of Workers' Compensation, I was injured at work

points.text: California Labor Commissioner youth brochure.
points.quote: Retaliation is illegal!
points.source: California Labor Commissioner's Office, Youth Advocate Program brochure

points.text: New York: no firing or punishment for reporting a problem.
points.quote: Your employer cannot fire or punish you for reporting a problem at your workplace.
points.source: New York State Department of Labor, Youth Worker Information Hub

points.text: Illinois Department of Labor: retaliation is against state law.
points.quote: It is against Illinois law for an employer to retaliate against a worker for exercising their rights
points.source: Illinois Department of Labor, File a Workplace Complaint

points.text: Illinois workers' compensation: no firing or harassing for claiming benefits.
points.quote: harass, discharge, refuse to rehire, or discriminate in any way against an employee
points.source: Illinois Workers' Compensation Commission, Handbook on Workers' Compensation

sections.title: 6. Who to call
sections.plain: Federal and state offices answer questions by phone. OSHA is for unsafe work. The Wage and Hour Division is for child labor and pay. The EEOC is for harassment and discrimination. Each state office below handles child labor, workers' compensation, or harassment in that state. Every number is copied from the page named under it. Two Georgia pages gave different Wage and Hour numbers, so for Georgia we list only the Georgia Child Labor Section and the national Wage and Hour number. Calling an office is not legal advice from us, and we cannot say what an office will tell you.

points.text: OSHA invites young workers to call with questions or to ask for an inspection.
points.quote: Call us on our toll-free number: 1-800-321-OSHA (6742) to get answers to your questions,
points.source: US OSHA, Safe Work for Young Workers

points.text: Wage and Hour helpline hours and number.
points.quote: call our toll-free information and helpline, available 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. in your time zone, 1-866-4USWAGE (1-866-487-9243).
points.source: US DOL Wage and Hour Division, Fact Sheet 43

points.text: DOL says complaints are free and private.
points.quote: Many investigations are initiated by complaints, which are free and confidential.
points.source: US DOL Wage and Hour Division, YouthRules

points.text: EEOC number for questions.
points.source: US EEOC, Tips for Youth @ Work

points.text: California: Division of Workers' Compensation live help.
points.quote: You can also call the DWC Information Services Center at 1-800-736-7401 to speak to a live representative.
points.source: California DIR, Division of Workers' Compensation

points.text: New York: help to file a complaint.
points.quote: If you need additional assistance to file your complaint, please call: 888-525-2267.
points.source: New York State Department of Labor, Youth Worker Information Hub

points.text: Illinois: the Illinois Department of Labor complaint page lists 312-793-5570 under child labor. The page says its Child Labor Law protects workers under 16.
points.quote: The Child Labor Law protects workers under the age of 16 by:
points.source: Illinois Department of Labor, File a Workplace Complaint

gaps: The EEOC pages we read do not say how old you must be to file a complaint.

The California pages we read do not say in plain words that a teen may refuse unsafe work. The Georgia and Illinois youth pages we read do not list a right to safe work or safety training. Only New York's page says a worker may say no to a task that risks serious injury or death.
We found no Georgia youth page about harassment or about punishment for speaking up, so this page makes no Georgia claim on those.
The California injured worker page, the Illinois workers' compensation handbook and the Georgia workers' compensation FAQ do not mention minors.
The Georgia workers' compensation documents are dated July 2019 and the Illinois handbook is dated January 2013. Ask the state office if the rule has changed.

Three official pages would not open for us: the New York Division of Human Rights page on sexual harassment (blocked) and two Illinois pages (not found). So there is no New York Division of Human Rights number here. The Illinois Department of Human Rights number comes only from the Illinois Department of Labor complaint page.
Two Georgia pages gave different Wage and Hour phone numbers, so we list only the national Wage and Hour number.
